subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING LABELLING OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
AMENDMENT RESPECTING LABELLING OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-176, to amend the Food and Drugs Act (labelling of dates on perishable commodities).

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING LABELLING OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING LABELLING OF CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to enable the consumer when shopping for food, drugs, cosmetics or other perishables to determine accurately that the product he or she buys will be as fresh as depicted by the advertising, labelling and packaging. It is becoming increasingly difficult, due to modern packaging methods, for the shopper to determine whether his or her selection has been on the retailer's shelf, in storage or transit for some time, thus causing the product to be at best stale and on some occasions injurious to health.
This bill would require all perishable products to be clearly marked as to the date the product was manufactured or produced and the ultimate date to which the product in question may be used without any danger to health.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the Minister of Transport.
The minister is no doubt aware of the proposed lay-off on November 1 by the Canadian National Railways of several hundred employees, including 22 in my riding. Could he tell us whether he and his department have taken steps to prevent these layoffs?

subsubtopic: PROSPECTIVE LAY-OFFS IN QUEBEC AND MARITIMES
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. Immediately on hearing this news I got in touch with the management of the Canadian National Railways, and they have advised me that the current reductions are part of the normal, continuing process of adjusting the size of the work force to meet the varying employment requirements. The fact is that train movements this year are down very substantially below those in the same period last year. Generally speaking, railway employment rises and falls in accordance with the work load resulting from such factors as seasonal needs, weather conditions, timing and progress in respect of capital projects, developing types of competition, operating and equipment requirements to meet traffic demands.
The government and the management of the C.N.R. are sensitive to the hardships which might result from work force adjustments and will take whatever steps are possible to improve the situation. It must be realized, of course, that unless operating costs are kept under control the company's competitive position will be jeopardized and along with it the continuing livelihood of all the employees.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks I should like to address to the minister on this occasion. He may perhaps recall that on November 4, 1964 I brought to his attention the matter of introducing into this country the metric system. He gave me what I thought was a very courteous hearing. I was endeavouring particularly to emphasize the point that if this system is to come into operation in this country, where it is not in use now except very slightly in a scientific way, a great deal of preparatory work will be required. My attention was directed to this matter at that time because Dr. Howlett had written an article which received a great deal of coverage. It emphasized to my mind the necessity for the introduction of this system. I tried to point out that based on my own experience I felt this was a very necessary and worth-while action, that it would simplify scientific work in the nation and would be of great help to the consumers who would find it would be much simpler to compare the cost of cans of food, butter and other articles that are commonly sold.
I had hoped that by this time in 1967, almost three years later, some evidence would be before us that the government had taken some steps to institute this system. I regret to say that I have seen none at all. I doubt that anybody else has either. This does not make the matter any less important. Therefore I should like to emphasize again, without going over all the evidence I did on that occasion, that the metric system is accepted practically all over the world. It would assist us greatly in our external trade and in the operation of business within the country if we used it. It would help the consumer and would help all students in this country because they would not be compelled to learn a very awkward and inefficient system. Instead, students could use a simple and efficient system in its place. I hope the minister will have some comments to make on this matter when he gets up to speak later in this debate.

Mr. Chairman, earlier this afternoon there was an attempt made on both sides of the house to discuss a serious situation in the
IThe Chairman.]
province of British Columbia. At the time I thought to myself that it really is closely connected with the business before us now. I should like to deal with it on the basis of the responsibility of this department and the minister for the situation which has arisen in the city of Victoria.
As was pointed out earlier today, the oldest shipbuilding firm on the west coast of Canada is closing at the end of the year having been sold to another shipbuilding firm, the Bur-rard Dry dock Company of North Vancouver. The new owners propose to shut down the firm in Victoria and cease its shipbuilding operations. In the announcement of the closure of this yard on the west coast the president, Mr. Harold Husband, reported he had had a report from a reliable source in Ottawa that the government was proposing to cancel its program for the building of vessels for the coastguard on the west coast of Canada. I do not know whether we shall ever be told what the policy of the government is in this regard or whether, as usual, we will have to wait for the evidence of its neglect to accumulate before our eyes.
What does strike me about this situation, however, is that not only has the government failed to go through with a program which has long been necessary but that there also is a much more serious failure on the part of the government to develop the Canadian economy. There is something fantastic and absurd in the spectacle of this very wealthy country apparently being unable to support a shipbuilding industry and unable apparently to support a merchant marine, when we compare Canada with that much smaller nation, Sweden, whose population is hardly more than one third that of Canada and which is today in the process of constructing new shipbuilding yards. We are not doing this for the simple reason, of course, that this government is not concerned about the development of a mature economy in Canada. It is much happier that the iron ore mined in the constituency of my seatmate, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, should be shipped to Japan. It is much happier not to have a steel industry established on the west coast and apparently is much happier that a gradual contraction is taking place on both sides of the country.
On the east coast the coal mines are being shut down and on the west coast shipbuilding is being shut down because the government has not undertaken its responsibilities with regard to the development of the Canadian economy. I am again reminded of
Ociober 30, 1967

the singular lack of enthusiasm displayed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce when I asked him, at a meeting of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, whether he did not consider that the first duty of the government is to ensure the development of the Canadian economy. The minister said that it was one of the responsibilities of the government but that the government had to be concerned also about our export trade.
I suggest that events such as the one in Victoria indicate it is time the government began to accept the role that government must play in the modern world. It is no longer sufficient for government, as this government seems to want to do all the time, merely to go through the motions of being a referee between contending forces in our society. That age is gone. It now is time for the government to become a player in the economic game of the country.
Yesterday I was interested to learn through the press of a report, which emanated from mysterious sources in the same way all such reports do, to the effect that the government has in mind a role for the Canada Development Corporation which will be very different from that envisaged by the former minister of finance, the present President of the Privy Council. The report suggested that the Canada Development Corporation would play some part in the restructuring of Canadian industry for which members in this party have been pressing for two years now. I shall be interested to see how far the government will go in this regard. It may be that the government at last is awaking to the necessity to take action to develop our own economy.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I would suggest in respect of the closing of the Victoria Machinery Depot, which will take place apparently because the Burrard Drydock Company does not consider it worth keeping open inasmuch as the government has failed to go through with its plans for a coastguard service and is still leaving us dependent on the U.S. coastguard service, although in the face of an emergency it will couple together the air force, the towboat companies and various other interests, that the government should proceed with its program of coastguard vessel construction. I suggest it is time the government took a look at this situation. I suggest that as a first step it should re-establish the shipbuilding industry on the west coast and, for that matter, on the east coast, and that it should go through
Supply-Industry
with the coastguard vessel construction program. It should adopt a program of building new and more up to date vessels to service lighthouses and for buoy marking, which according to the report has also been cancelled. The government should take definite steps to encourage the development of a steel industry on the west coast of Canada where there are the natural resources to support it and where we obviously have a need for the steel that could be produced there.
One of the difficulties the shipbuilding industry of British Columbia has been facing is that in my province the workers com-mendably have been able to extract more satisfactory wages from their employers than workers in the same industry on the east coast and in central Canada have. Their wages are about a dollar an hour more than wages in eastern or central Canada. Even more important has been the cost of transporting components and steel supplies from central and eastern Canada. This is a clear indication that this government has abdicated its role of governing in the modern age and is going to let the whole economy wither on the vine. It merely exemplifies what a correspondent of mine had to say in a letter I received from him. He is a Canadian newspaper correspondent stationed abroad, and he remarked that in looking at his own country from abroad it occurred to him that the government is allowing the economy to veer like a tank completely out of control from one ditch to another in the hope it will be able to avoid complete catastrophe by doing nothing and by refusing to take the driver's seat in making the economy move forward in the twentieth century and into the twenty first.
It appears that this government is much more concerned about having this country as an adjunct or ancillary to our great friend next door. I am sure it considers there is something wrong in developing a forceful and viable economy of our own because it does nothing whatever to encourage it and everything to discourage it. This is just another example of the results of the government's inaction.
It is my hope that the government will not allow too many more plants to shut down because we are going to see a picture of despair in the form of the minister of manpower who valiantly tries to slip men into new slots as the slots they are now in close behind them. The slots are closing all over the country today and very soon the minister of manpower will be in the position of not being able to place these displaced people in

October 30. 1967
Supply-Industry
our economy, particularly if his colleagues who determine and control the over-all economy are permitted to have their way.
I hope the warning signals now flying in Nova Scotia and British Columbia alert the Canadian people to the dangers of leaving their affairs in the hands of a government which refuses to govern, a government, indeed, whose philosophy is that government is best when it does the least governing and interferes as little as possible. This is a government which is committed entirely to an outmoded doctrinaire system which no longer exists, that of free enterprise.
The people of Canada are now paying a huge price for this attitude and the people of my province are going to pay a very high price as a result of this example of governmental neglect to stabilize and remedy the situation that resulted in the closing of this shipyard. I am afraid this may only be the first in a series of closures which may result in the most drastic economic decline in Canada. This will surely happen unless the government finally summons the courage and intelligence to start governing and directing the economy, as only the government can in this day and age.
I have received telegrams from people in Victoria who are greatly distressed by this situation and hope we can do something to avert this local tragedy. I do not suppose we can avert it. I have no doubts whatever that the government knew very well it was not going to go ahead with the building program which might have kept this shipyard in existence. I have no doubt it has known this for many months but has done nothing about it. The government has not even warned the unfortunate victims of its folly, as was the case in respect of Dosco. If the government did not know this was going to happen, all I can say is, this is further proof that the government is thoroughly incompetent and unfit to control the affairs of Canada.

To Sydney, where the furniture is transshipped to Newfoundland, the rate is to go from $5.36 to $17.78 for a chesterfield suite, that is, a chesterfield and a chair.

It seems to me that the Department of Industry should be equally as alert to prevent the demise of industries as it is to encourage new industry.
I come back to my original point, the one made by the hon. member for Bow River. I believe that the Minister of Industry should make it a point to play an effective role with his colleagues in seeing that these proposed freight rates are not put into effect. I again refer to the point made by the hon. member for Waterloo South and his criticism of allowing crises to occur. This is just the sort of thing that should be avoided, and I believe the province of Nova Scotia and probably all the maritime provinces will be very alert in watching to see what is done in this regard.
I should like to spend a moment discussing the fishery, the main industry of my area. Here again, through lack of co-ordination the growth of the industry is being severely circumscribed because of the lack of increased facilities in the infrastructure of the industry. I have here a copy of the Yarmouth newspaper with a picture of the public wharf just after it was built. I believe it was completed in 1964. The picture shows that there was at that time a normal amount of shipping around the wharf. A picture taken during the first week of October shows that you cannot see the wharf for ships. The seiners and trawlers are clustered around it, and in places these ships are six or seven deep. Obviously crowding to this extent inhibits efficient fishing operations. I take this opportunity of calling to the attention of the Minister of Industry the fact that here is an industry whose growth is being impeded by inadequate facilities. I also point out that this is occurring in an area where the economy is fragile.
The laying off of 70 or 80 men in a constituency such as mine, in an area such as the one in which the furniture factory to
Supply-Industry
which I have referred is located, is equivalent to the laying off of thousands in a larger area. I ask the Minister of Industry to make it a point in his dealings with his colleagues to emphasize the need to avoid freight rate increases that are out of all proportion and will have the effect of killing the existing industries that we have. I also emphasize the necessity of providing new facilities and the enlargement of existing facilities where this is necessary because of the growth of industry.

Mr. Chairman, there are a few brief comments I should like to make in connection with these estimates. One of my colleagues say that is a refreshing change, but I understand there is agreement that these estimates will be passed by five o'clock and I know that other hon. members wish to participate in the debate. Therefore it is not possible, as I would have liked to have done, to review this interesting department, but I know how much the minister enjoys sitting in the house and listening in his genial, friendly and co-operative manner to comments from the opposition.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
However, I cannot but hark back to the birth of this department. It was an event likened to the coming of the second messiah. It was the great new department which was going to cure all our problems, rationalize all Canadian industry and implement adjustments in the automotive industry. It would also take care of any trade adjustments under the Kennedy round. In short, it would do everything in a wonderful way.
The minister has learned the great art practised in Otttawa. Not only does he know his way around as a former deputy minister but he has also developed the political techniques of how to build an empire. The size of this department has increased in a completely inverse ratio to its accomplishments. It has trebled in size. No matter what we on this side of the house say the minister goes about in a lively way surrounded by his prize whiz kids and determined to preserve his view that the opposition are a bunch of dunderheads who really do not know anything anyway. He merely tolerates us as his estimates go through the house.
I would have liked to go through his department in detail but we had a good go at it last time and I know the minister must get away. As I said, I am not sure it would be productive or that there would be any real purpose in doing so. As an empire builder

the minister is wonderful. He has out-Cae-sared Caesar himself, at least so far as the growth of the department is concerned.
I want to say a word or two about the automotive pact which, as the minister knows, is my perennially favourite subject. If he does not have an opportunity to answer a couple of points I wish to raise, perhaps some of the departmental officials might send me some information about them if it exists. We are told on good authority that great pressure is being exerted by the United States government, the United States motor car companies and their subsidiaries in Canada for a drastic reduction in the Canadian content under the agreement with the possible goal of eliminating it entirely. If this is true we should know about it. It is not necessarily a bad thing if it is prepared for. If there is a sufficient competitive advantage on each side it may be a desirable end. However, I hope the government will not keep it a secret until the last moment as it has done with everything else under this agreement.
I hope the government will make this type of information available. I realize that at least in the initial years some built-in protection is perhaps necessary under the agreement but it may be that it is possible to reduce it later and perhaps in time remove it. I would like to hear the minister's comment in this regard. However, we know there is pressure from the United States and we should like to know its source and strength and the government's likely response to it.
I think that in one area the agreement has been a total failure. Everyone admits that employment has increased in the automotive industry and that because of changes dislocations are not as great as they were. In fact I think there was only one case this year. It occurred in the Chrysler company and it was not really serious. Of course we do not know whether the general expansion in the automotive industry would have taken place in any event. But in one area, that of prices, the agreement seems to be a failure.
When the agreement was approved by parliament some years ago one of its great selling points, both inside the house and more specifically outside the house as stated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, was that it would ultimately result in a reduction in prices and that the advantages given to the companies under the agreement would in a reasonable space of time be passed on to the public in the form of lower automobile prices. We heard of the $50 million which the

poor, debt-ridden General Motors Corporation and the others needed to build new plants. They needed it like a hole in the head but they got it just the same. The straw which was thrown to us was the statement that this would bring about lower prices. This did not happen. The public has been sold out by the government. Prices have not come down. The consumer has not benefited in any real way. The disparity in prices has not narrowed, as we were told it would, and the promise that the public would benefit has not been fulfilled.
Why does the minister not take the one obvious step which would accomplish this? For several years now we have asked the government to remove the tariff on automobile imports as it applies to individuals. It is true that the companies have this advantage, but why does he not give it to everyone else? This would be the most effective way of forcing the motor car companies to reduce their prices. If they did not want to do it all one would have to do if one lived near the border would be to drive over to Buffalo and buy a car there and the $200 one saved would give one a good week end while over there. I do not understand why the government continues to sell the public short and will not take any steps to remedy this situation.
The other question I should like to put to the minister is with regard to his position on trade adjustment assistance. To what degree is this matter dealt with by the Department of Trade and Commerce? We have been told for years now that Canada's salvation lies in the trade adjustments taking place under the Kennedy tariff cuts. We also know that in the short run this may well mean a significant hardship for Canadians. Many of our small industries which have grown up behind tariff walls will probably die when these walls are blown away by the new trade winds. We have never been able to get a commitment from the government for a trade adjustment act and genuine trade adjustment assistance. What is the position of the department in this regard?
I know that the Department of Industry has cannibalized many other departments to build its own staff but how will it co-ordinate its work with, for example, the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Finance in order to convince not just the business community but labour and the municipalities which have just as big a stake in whatever industrial changes will take place? It is not good enough for the minister
October 30, 1967

to run around the country holding conferences with business alone. Municipalities have great investments in these communities and there is a great capital debt built up. Unions have the investment of their men in these communities. I would like to know how the department will deal with the whole problem of trade assistance under the Kennedy tariff proposals in the next year or two.
Finally, I cannot help but make reference to Dosco in view of the minister's speech the other day in which he spoke about focusing on specific economic and technological problems, etc. These are very nice and good words. We have heard them from him ever since the department was established. I was in Sydney before the last general election attending a nomination meeting. I went down there primarily out of interest in the area. The economic problems of Dosco, its rundown equipment, its lack of proper markets, and the unwillingness of the owners to modernize and to seek other products and other markets have been known for five years. This has been a known fact both in that area and in Ottawa. I should like to know whether the department is taking a look at sick industries and, if so, what kind of studies are being made.
These are the only points I wish to raise and I believe they are relevant to the future of this department. I have never been impressed with the department. I am told that half of the whiz kids sit around in utter frustration because there is no real cohesion, no real direction from the minister in assigning projects. I know that many provincial representatives have given up because they cannot find what the department is studying when they come down here to talk to the department. It is all very hush, hush.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
There may be a place for this department. It seems to me that at the moment its status and its co-ordination with other important departments have not been defined, have not been effectively worked out. If we had the time I should like to spend a few hours with the minister asking him for more specific answers to some of these questions. As I say, the minister may be able to satisfy us on these points. I hope he will at least try. With these words we will let the minister go for another year.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to put a couple of questions to the minister, one of a general nature and one of a more specific nature.
Supply-Industry
I am bound to say also that in putting the questions I appreciate the fact that all members of the committee are in the same difficult position as I am because of the ridiculous 30-day limitation on the discussion of supply. We find now that we have two and a half days left for discussion of the estimates of several important departments. A number of members make general remarks as well as asking specific questions. These take the whole of the one day now allotted to each remaining department, so the minister is able to ride it out comfortably by simply sitting there and not dealing with our questions. Then, if there are any objections that by the end of the day he has not answered any questions, he says there were so many members who had things to say, that he wanted to hear everything they had to say, and the time allowed expired before he was able to answer questions.
The result will be that members who have had serious questions to ask are left without answers as a result of these rules. Another result of this situation will be that some time Thursday hundreds of millions of dollars, probably billions of dollars of estimates will be passed in a few minutes, the subject matter of many of which have not even been referred to, let alone discussed in committee of supply. Discussion of the estimates will be closed and scores, if not hundreds, of questions that have been asked will be left unanswered.
As I say, the Minister of Industry is not responsible for this rule. However, I feel it is important we should point up the situation as I am doing now, because the position it leaves this committee of supply in has now been amply demonstrated so that it should be obvious to everybody that the continuation of this rule should neither be sought nor acceded to if it is sought. In addition, I should like to suggest to the minister with regard to his current estimates that he should consider following the course of answering questions as they are addressed to him, even although there may be other speeches to be made later and other questions to be asked later.
This brings me to my question. I should like to ask the minister if he can tell us whether any appreciable change is contemplated at the moment in the list or composition of the designated areas across the country? I may as well tell the minister that there have been rumours that he is contemplating making an important statement in the very near future in which he will say that a review has been made and the situation of a

number ol designated areas has improved to the point where they can now be-how will I put it-de-designated. I am asking the minister whether in fact he is contemplating any such move. If so, will he take the committee into his confidence today by giving us a list of such areas and a summary of the progress made as well as the reasons these areas are to be removed from the list?
Second, I should like to renew a request I made of the minister with regard to my own area of Kamloops and particularly the district of Merritt within that area. In my constituency, sir, we are immediately adjacent to another splendid area of British Columbia, the Okanagan valley. I should make it clear that the Thompson valley in which Kamloops is and the Okanagan valley are contiguous but they are not the same, although their physical, geographic and economic bases are very much the same. However, we find ourselves in my district in a non-desig-nated area whereas the Okanagan-I may say to everybody's surprise including initially that of the premier of the province-is at least the first of not the only area of British Columbia which was designated. I may say that Premier Bennett was greatly surprised to be told that his home town area, including Kelowna, was designated as the poorest or as having a standard of income lower than any other part of British Columbia. However, I believe Premier Bennett has been able to reconcile himself to that designation because it has been found to be of substantial benefit to the Okanagan.
But the result has been that industries which have been contemplating settling somewhere in the interior of British Columbia have, understandably, all gone to the Okanagan area. May I say to the minister in all sincerity that I have been asked to take up this matter by my constituents, not in the spirit of a dog in the manger saying that he should take designation from the Okanagan and give it to the Kamloops area. On the contrary, we are happy if it is helping them, but if you feel you must leave them as they are, then you must also designate the Kamloops area which has the same basic geographic and economic features.
There have been at least two specific instances which have concerned our people in the Kamloops area, where industries which had first been considering settling in Kamloops have been attracted to the Okanagan area by these various incentives. The two areas are only 70 miles apart, but as they have the same access to markets, the same
IMr. Fulton.]
availability of labour and so on, it is only natural that with the incentives the industries have gone to the Okanagan area. Kamloops businessmen are now having to compete with subsidized businesses in the Okanagan area.
Those people on whose behalf I am speaking are not resentful of the good fortune that has come to the Okanagan by virtue of being designated. We do say, however, that it was never the basic intention to create such discrimination between two immediately adjacent areas as results from designating the one area and not designating the other. So I repeat my request to the minister that the Kamloops area be designated. Indeed, early this spring when we had the matter under discussion by way of correspondence, the minister said that the whole basis for designating areas was to be reviewed and that he would be in touch with me after that. I hope that as a result of the review he will be able to tell me that the Kamloops area will be designated.
Within this area there is the particular district of Merritt, which suffers from the economic disadvantage of having had a decline in employment in the area. The town is primarily dependent upon the Craigmont mine, a strip mining operation which has been closed, and upon a number of lumbering industries which will suffer a further decline in employment in the near future as a result of having their allowable quotas cut under the provincial forest regulations. Merritt now has an emergency situation. If we are to retain any sort of control of our own economy such a corporation must be put into operation. Let me give several examples of recent Canadian mineral developments which might have been retained in Canadian hands had a natural resources development corporation been on the statute books. Perhaps the most dramatic example is the Rainbow oil field in Alberta.

If we participated in this manner in no way would we interfere with private enterprise. We would co-operate with private enterprise, and quite obviously it would be an easy matter in most cases to arrange for

the preferential participation of Canadians in such developments. But in some cases our partners would be foreign governments or foreign companies. I do not think many people realize that 35 per cent of the Canadian land mass lies within the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. Experts predict that not too long from now, with a substantial increase in exploration in these areas, it is reasonable to expect that 35 per cent of Canada's mineral resources will be found in these territories. I would like to see greater Canadian participation in these discoveries. Apart from the very obvious reason that the creation of a natural resources corporation will give the Canadian people a more important piece of the action in this field, we will be able to retain in Canadian hands a much larger percentage of our resources than we do now. Even more important, it will give us a more important sense of participation in our national development.
What is more important is that if such a program by a development corporation is applied with particular emphasis to the Yukon and the Northwest Territories it will dramatize a basis for national unity which far too few people in this country and more particularly in my province of Quebec appreciate, namely, the fact that the natural resources of these two areas of Canada, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, are commonly owned and are the common heritage of all Canadians. Unlike the situation within the provinces where the provinces own the natural resources within their boundaries, all the Canadian people control and own the fantastic natural resources of these two territories.
In closing I would simply like to reiterate what I said earlier, that as a young Canadian I want to see the Canadian people participate much more fully than they have to date in the development of the mineral resources of this country. If we restrict the new development corporation initially to the Northwest Territories and the Yukon and to mineral and oil development in these areas we will be able to start tomorrow because the provinces would offer no objection and I cannot imagine any real criticism of such an action

Supply-Industry
by private industry. In fact I think the Canadian mineral industry as a whole, except possibly for the very large corporations which have tremendous capital resources of their own, would be delighted to see the government make funds available for the development of proven ore bodies. The hon. member for Saint John-Albert asked a number of questions about the designated area program. He asked particularly about Saint John. His first question was whether federal assistance has been a deciding factor in the location of new industries in the Atlantic provinces or has been of assistance in the relocation of industries in that area. The answer of course is that this program has been a not inconsiderable factor in inducing new manufacturing and processing industries to locate in the maritimes. Figures have already been given. As a consequence of this program, since its inception until September 30 last some 78 projects have been undertaken in the hon. member's province of New Brunswick, involving the expenditure of approximately $202 million. These projects have provided new job opportunities for approximately 4,800 employees.
Whether federal assistance has had any effect on the relocation of industries within the maritimes may best be answered this way. As the hon. member knows, the program is designed to avoid the shifting of existing industries from one point to another. A requirement, if there is to be a benefit under the program, is that 95 per cent of the capital facilities to be installed in any plant which is moved to a designated area must be new machinery and equipment. The purpose of this provision is to prevent the mere physical transfer of old plant and equipment from a non-designated area to a designated area. The idea is that unless an entrepreneur wishes to set up a new plant and equipment he will have no reason to shift. We know of

October 30, 1967
Supply-Industry
two relocations where industries have moved to designated areas in the maritimes as a consequence of this program.
One instance is the G. E. Barbour Company Limited which was forced to move from its location in Saint John. Because of the purchase of land and buildings by the Saint John bridge authority it was no longer possible for that firm to continue where it was. In seeking a new location they decided to move from an area of relatively good employment to an area of chronic unemployment, at the same time qualifying for benefits.
A similar sort of thing took place in the instance of Marden-Wild of Canada Limited in Halifax. This firm was no longer able to continue in business because of rezoning which was carried out in Halifax and they moved from Halifax to a designated area.
The hon. member also asked how many applications for assistance from industry have been rejected because of inability to relocate in growth centres. I do not know what the hon. member means by growth centres. I cannot think of any manufacturing or processing industry which would have to locate in an urban area such as Halifax or Saint John and, if there were sufficient financial attractions, could not locate outside those areas. Outside these two main centres that I have referred to there are a number of other manufacturing areas which are adequately provided with labour, communications and public utilities.
The hon. member asked why Saint John has not been designated and whether there is any hope that it will be designated. The designated areas program is designed to induce entrepreneurs in Canada who wish to set up new manufacturing or processing industries to set them up in areas of chronic unemployment. The idea is to bring relief to those areas of Canada where unemployment figures are highest. The program attempts to provide more employment opportunities for those who live in areas of chronic unemployment and seeks to induce industry to designated areas rather than to those areas where the unemployment situation perhaps is not so acute.
Saint John is fortunate in terms of relative unemployment. In the past ten years it has experienced a not unsatisfactory rate of economic growth. As the hon. gentleman knows, the average non-farm family income also is at a satisfactory level. Until-and I hope this will never happen-Saint John has the misfortune to register a much higher level of

unemployment than is current now, I should not think there is much prospect that it will be designated. I am sure the hon. member shares my hope that designation for Saint John will never be necessary.

question? I thank the minister for his answers. Has subsection 9(e) of the legislation been used? I might point out that a large part of the expenditures on the Avro Arrow were incurred not in connection with research but for production models. It was only after substantial expenditure had been incurred in connection with preproduction that the government of the day decided not to go ahead with the program. One should not assume that all the sums of money which have been mentioned in connection with this particular program were spent on research and development. The second example the hon. member gave was that of the Bobcat. This is clearly a situation of the kind one must expect to encounter in any developmental program. It did not turn out to be a good guess.
As to the hydrofoil a considerable amount of research and development has been done in connection with this project. The work suffered a setback as the result of a fire which occurred some time ago, but research and development are continuing. If the hon. gentleman has information to the effect that this effort has been cancelled, neither my colleague the Minister of National Defence nor I have any knowledge of it. In any event, the fact that sums of money are spent on research and development in connection with items which do not reach the production stage does not necessarily mean that all the money is wasted. There is in connection with all these programs a considerable industrial fall-out.

Supply-Industry
There have, of course, been a number of successful programs under the defence export development program to which the hon. member referred. Since my administration of it began, at any rate, we have been spending at the rate of about $20 million or $22 million a year. Since its inception 109 defence development projects have been supported from this vote and expenditures to date amount to $103 million. Of the projects supported, 53 in number costing $53 million have been completed and are achieving sales. So for $53 million we get some results.
I intend to mention some of them. The value of the sales or orders resulting from these projects is $348 million. Here are some figures by way of example: the PT-6 turbine engine, $58 million; the Doppler navaid, $115 million; the GRC-103 radio relay, $18 million; the Buffalo STOL aircraft, $49 million; the twin Otter aircraft, $25 million; the CL-89 Drone, $60 million; flight simulators for both military and civil aircraft, $15 million. So for an investment of some $53 million in these projects resulting sales are in excess of $388 million. This does not mean that every project we bet on is going to turn out well. Some do not turn out well. Either the scientists have endeavoured to accomplish too big a task and been unsuccessful, or they have been unable to move as fast as other people and we have lost a particular race, or the need for a particular object under development has in the course of time, some four or five years, disappeared.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
In an effort to avoid this we obtain the best possible advice concerning what is technologically and scientifically a good bet. We try to ensure that this is put into the hands of the most competent developers in the country. All these programs are kept under continuous review. Once there is any indication that a project will be unsuccessful it is stopped. We had occasion to make reference to one the other day. A gas turbine engine was being developed in Toronto. When it appeared clear that further developmental expenditures would not yield a return this development work was stopped and the people were put to work on something else. I suggest there is some management being carried out in respect of these programs.
The hon. gentleman, among others, mentioned the situation in respect of the closing of the Victoria Machinery Depot. This is most unfortunate. It represents perhaps rather

more than just the closing of the oldest shipyard in British Columbia. It represents the consolidation of the shipbuilding element of V.M.D. with those of Burrard and Yarrows. It is my understanding that these three units or two, because the control of Yarrows and Burrard is the same, will now be run as one unit.
I think it is a source of regret that in respect of shipbuilding yards which have the capacity to build or repair very large ships we should have lost an element of competition which existed hitherto. It is difficult to generate competition if the entrepreneurs who provide it are not persuaded that it is a good thing.
It has been alleged that the reason for the closing down was the failure of the government of Canada to proceed with its shipbuilding program. I should point out that a little over two years ago we did disclose to the shipbuilding industry in Canada a five year program of government shipbuilding; it was all laid out. It was declared then that competition for this program would be on a national basis. However, in order to enable a transition to be made from the old system to the new, shipbuilding companies on the west coast were guaranteed that the west coast would be free of competition from the rest of Canada for certain ships. Reference has been made to a recent report based on the assumption that the Department of Transport should or would build a couple of coastguard cutters which were not included in this transitional program. Now it appears to have been learned from somewhere that these two ships which were not in the plan in the first place are not going to be built. Mr. Chairman, I see that we have now exceeded the allotted time.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act so that workmen may deduct from their taxable income any expense incurred by the acquisition of hand or electrical tools required to perform their work.

He said: Mr. Speaker, notice of motion No. 12 appearing on the order paper could apply to all workers entered on a payroll.
As I have already mentioned on several occasions in this house, we are allowing a general discrimination against workers with regard to employers or to all those who are not wage earners. Besides, one could say generally that tax deduction at the source is a glaring injustice towards workmen, as compared to other groups. Moreover, I have already pointed out in this house that a wage earner entered on a payroll is not given the same advantages, because his income tax is deducted from his gross earnings and he is not allowed the same deductions as a businessman or a professional or any other worker not entered on a payroll.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
I have already said, in this house, that the worker has the right, just as anyone else, to file his income tax return at the end of the year without being deprived of the amount deducted each pay day from his gross salary.
I believe it was claimed, at the time, that this would be hard to do but I feel the difficulty has been overcome, due to the fact that the worker still has to file his income tax return at the end of the year to claim the excess money the government has taken from him. In other words, the government paid itself first, and once again the worker has to
Income Tax Act
defend himself, as best he can, against the government that dipped into his gross salary.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I ask the government to amend that famous Income Tax Act to allow workers, and members of the various trades, to deduct the cost of the tools they need to do their work.
I have in mind, for instance, service station mechanics, carpenters, lumberjacks, while professionals, such as dentists and others, are entitled to deduct from their taxable income purchase and maintenance costs for their equipment as well as travel and other costs related to their profession. I feel that this exemption is quite justified, and I approve it.
Similarly, large corporations engaged in developing our natural resources given over to them by our governments for practically nothing, benefit from tax exemptions on all capital equipment, which amount to millions of dollars.
I am not against such tax exemptions inasmuch, and I do say, inasmuch as the same tax privileges are granted to labourers for necessary expenses related to their work. That is why ever since I came to this house I have been asking for a similar exemption, particularly for the workers of the province of Quebec who have to buy a power saw and pay for the cost of parts, and God knows how many they need, for a small machine which works so hard. If one adds to that, the cost of gasoline, oil, and so on, one can easily realize that it costs about $1,000 to $1,500 per season for the purchase and the maintenance of that equipment.
There is also the cost of safety clothes which the governments force the loggers to buy and wear in order to protect their lives. Let us add to that travelling expenses for the long distance they have to cover sometimes to get to their work, and we shall easily reach expenses of at least $2,000 a year for an ordinary bush worker.

Income Tax Act

subtopic: SUGGESTED DEDUCTION BY WORKMEN OF EXPENDITURES FOR HAND OR ELECTICAL TOOLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the notice of motion of the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act so that workmen may deduct from their taxable income any expense incurred by the acquisition of hand or electrical tools required to perform their work.
The house is asked from time to time to grant employees tax exemptions for the cost of the equipment they need to do their work.
During the debate on the Income Tax Act in 1965, the then minister of finance, the hon. Mr. Gordon, was asked about that. He said that he was sympathetic to the requests and that he was not satisfied with the present provisions, adding however that because of the complexity of the whole matter he felt that a decision should be postponed until the government had at its disposal the recommendations of the royal commission on taxation.
Under the present act, employees cannot deduct the amounts spent on the purchase of tools needed for their work. It would be discriminatory to allow the bush workers to deduct the amounts spent on the hand, electric, or power tools they need for their work without granting the same deduction to all employees.
If such a deduction were allowed, it would imply a review of the whole question of deductions for expenses incurred in the course of employment, for instance, for the purchase of hand, electric or power tools, special uniforms, clothing and equipment needed by a workman to perform his work.
Even though several of those expenses must necessarily be made in the course of employment, in some cases it may be difficult

to determine whether a particular expense has been incurred for employment or personal purposes, for instance, in the case of the purchase of special clothing.
This whole matter should be discussed when the fiscal legislation is reviewed following the recommendations of the royal commission on taxation, instead of extending the provisions of the present legislation in a piecemeal fashion.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
The proposed amendment, if passed, would be difficult to apply. For example, although the hon. member explained in part what is meant by the word "workmen", does this term include tradesmen, lumbermen, mechanics, carpenters, bricklayers, masons, electricians, plumbers, teachers and the other professions? Why is the proposed deduction limited to expenses incurred by the acquisition of hand or electrical tools? Why does it not apply also to mechanical tools?
In the United States, the employee is generally considered as being in business and, under clause 162 of the internal revenue code, he is entitled to the same ordinary and necessary business expenses as the businessman or the professional who works for himself. The main difference between the expenses of a businessman and those of an employee is that the former can deduct all his ordinary and necessary expenses and still benefit from the ordinary reduction, while the employee who wishes to benefit by the ordinary reduction can claim only expenses falling in the four following categories: Reimbursed expenses, expenses for travel away from home, transportation expenses and travelling salesman expenses.
However, the employee may deduct other ordinary and necessary expenses instead of taking advantage of the ordinary reduction. The returns contain minute and severe conditions.
Mr. Speaker, another aspect of the expenses incurred in earning one's life which should be considered is that of transportation expenses. Many people today have to travel 40 to 80 miles to get to work. Some may say that these people should move closer to their work, but there may be good reasons why they cannot do so: they may be taking care of their parents, they may be home owners, or there may be some other reason.
And so, one finds it harder and harder, in the big cities, to buy a lot at a reasonable price for home building purposes. If income
October 30, 1367

tax law gave a deduction of these expenses from gross income, perhaps many people would act and build themselves a house in semi-urban or rural areas, which would alleviate the administrations of those large cities of many problems and would also make it possible for more people to acquire their own house, at a more reasonable price.
Here, Mr. Speaker, are some observations and related proposals made by the royal commission on taxation in its report, and I quote from page 289 of volume 3:
We now turn to consider the deduction of expenses by employees. The principle involved is clear enough. All of the expenses incurred in the expectation of generating net gains, other than personal living expenses, should be allowed as deductions from all actual gross gains. Distinctions between the kinds and forms of taxable gains, and considerations of whether a net gain actually resulted from the expenditures, are irrelevant. The major problem would be to allow the deduction of all expenses laid out to generate employment income and yet to prevent the deduction of personal living expenses.
It would be obvious in most cases, Mr. Speaker, as stated by the Carter report, that a given item falls within one category or the other, but marginal cases would be difficult to solve.
In this regard, the Carter report states the following in volume 3, page 316:
Because of the stringent limitations in the present law, employees are unable to deduct many expenses that are deductible by the self-employed. Skilled manual workers and employed professionals in particular are unfairly treated relative to the self-employed.
On page 312, volume 3, of the report of the royal commission on taxation, we find the proposed rules for deductibility, and I quote:
We came to the conclusion that the most equitable course would be to treat employment income on the same basis as income from a business or profession.
Expenses would then be deductible if reasonably related to the earning of income. The prohibition against the deduction of personal and living expenses as set out in section 12 (1)	(h) of the
Income Tax Act would, of course, be applicable, as would the provision in section 12	(2) that
expenses must be reasonable in the circumstances.
The adoption of such a course would remove the unfair discrimination between the two kinds of income and should not lead to much additional litigation. As we have already stated, the United States does place employment income on the same basis as business income, and all "ordinary and necessary" expenses are deductible for both kinds of income.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion before us, both the original and as amended. If I have any criticism to make with respect to the main motion or the amendment it is that the motion is still not comprehensive enough. Certainly the inclusion of the words proposed by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Keays) does make the resolution more worthy. The hon. member for Gaspe might have included one more feature in his amendment, and that would be certain kinds of work clothes that are necessary, such as hard hats, safety boots, and so on as used in certain occupations by construction workers. It is a matter, I suppose of making changes to the definitions in the Income Tax Act in order to cover certain types of safety clothes, helmets and so on.
In the little time available to me, I want to say that the point conjured up by the debate is the obvious one that the existing income tax law seems definitely to militate against the wage earner and salaried worker in this country. It seems to me the act obviously is of benefit to those who earn their income from fees and militates against those who earn their income from wages or salaries. In conversation earlier today the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said his interpretation of the income tax law could be set forth in a few words, namely that there is complete bias in the income tax legislation which has the effect of making it class legislation.

October 30, 1967
Income Tax Act
I am not for one moment trying to say that this was the intention, but it certainly has been the result. Our income tax law does not permit these people to deduct their expenses in acquiring the tools that are necessary for them to earn their livelihood. I believe the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Clermont) has already pointed out that the Carter commission report made specific recommendations in connection with this matter. It set forth three basic principles with regard to the new criteria which should be established with regard to determining in the future what expenses should be allowed.
I should like to put on the record these three principles, and I quote from page 83 of the Carter commission report:
The first general rule is that expenditures should be deductible only if they are reasonably related to the gaining or producing of income.
As a corollary of that first principle there is a second rule stated at page 85, which reads:
The second general rule is related to the first and would assert that expenditures otherwise deductible should not be allowed to the extent that they are unreasonable in the circumstance.
So we have injected into this consideration the premise of reasonableness of the amount of the deduction. Finally, Mr. Speaker, according to the Carter report, page 85, there is this third general rule:
The third general rule is that expenditures of a personal nature, that is expenditures made for personal use or consumption, should not be deductible.
No one is disagreeing with that in so far as the motion before us is concerned. Finally, on page 86 of the report there is in a sense a summary of the commission's thinking, which reads:
We have suggested that there should be a more liberal approach than currently exists to employee expense deductions.
I then add in parenthesis that when the commission uses the word "liberal" I take it the word is not used in a partisan sense.
We believe that the best way to achieve an equitable treatment of expenses related to employment is generally to apply the same rules to these expenditures as are to be applied to business expenditures.
I pause again to say that this seems to sum it up almost with perfection.
Thus, the present prohibition on the deduction of most employment expenses should be withdrawn, and the three rules outlined above should apply.
This report goes on to make reference to reducing the administrative problems of

accounting in connection with this matter. The report states that perhaps an optional standard deduction of 3 per cent of employment income, with a maximum deduction of $500, could be established. I believe some consideration of this matter indicates that most craftsmen, whether they be journeymen electricians or carpenters, make an initial expenditure of at least $300 or $400 for a basic set of tools necessary to their trade. Considering the inflation factor presently at work, it would seem that the figure put forward in the report is not unrealistic. In fact I believe the proposal before us, coupled with the recommendations in the Carter commission report, is very sensible and worthy of consideration. I cannot understand why these principles cannot be reflected in our legislation. As a matter of fact my colleagues, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) have almost every year for the past five years introduced private members bills or notices of motion calling for the same kind of change in our income tax laws as that proposed by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier).
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that, as a layman in income tax matters, when one looks with some detachment at our income tax law he finds there are certain basic injustices. For example professional men such as dentists or doctors are allowed deductions from income tax for the purchase of equipment. Let us take a dentist, for example. When he buys an electric drill which is necessary to earn his income, that expense is deductible, but when a carpenter buys an electric saw, which is equally necessary for him to earn his livelihood, that expense is not deductible. I might add that while some dentists are quite gentle and soothing in their work, it should be said that others lack precision in the use of their drills, just as some carpenters do in the use of their saws.

I should like to sum up my contribution to this debate by saying that we should accept the principle that if occupational necessity demands the use of a tool or set of tools, the capital required to purchase those tools should be deductible for income tax purposes in the same way as are tools used by those engaged in a professional occupation. To do otherwise it seems to me is to help perpetrate an economic injustice today.

I think all the points which have been brought out so effectively by my colleagues who have preceded me have been considered in the past by the authorities, and the real reason that change has not taken place heretofore is the difficulty of administration, which is a very real problem.
However, Mr. Speaker, we appreciate that while the Carter commission does not declare government policy, it does open up this field to new and enterprising examination. Currently, the Department of Finance is studying all of the Carter commission recommendations, as well as comments made by citizens in relation thereto, which come from all possible sources. I am sure that the debate which has been introduced so imaginatively by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) will contribute to this consideration.
The only commitment made so far by the government as I understand it, is the implementation of tax reform. The actual nature of this reform and the direction it may take is something that is at yet unannounced. I suppose the only question before us is the timeliness of taking remedial action before total tax revision.
There is one aspect that I should like to touch on which relates to the type of equipment that might be deductible from employment income for income tax purposes-what we might call tools of the trade. The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Schreyer) suggested a maximum of $500, but personally I think the figure might well be double that.
I should like to mention briefly some of the kinds of items that today would be very appropriate for consideration. Circular saws of six pounds to 16 pounds, in sizes of from six inches to ten inches, range in cost from $80 to $180. Quarter inch to lj-inch drills sell for from $12 to $200. So you can see that two or three of these items alone amount to a fairly substantial packet. Jig saws range in price from $20 to $100. Routers, which are rated in horsepower from half-horse to 21, horsepower, can cost anywhere from $50 to $250. Sanders, belt-type or finishing-type, range in price from $20 to $200.

The only person who got any credit for getting that deep water harbour constructed was the former member of parliament for the constituency, a man who unfortunately was defeated.
I know the minister would not approve of this. Had he been there he would not have said those things. He is not a politician.
A statesman.
However, I sat there listening to all the great things that had been done by my predecessor.
Oh, oh.

I would like to remind the hon. member who was interjecting that if he had been in this house from 1958 to 1962 and seen the work done by the then hon. member for Gaspe he would be in a position to say today that it was a Conservative government which
[Mr. KeaysJ
approved the project, and that it was a Liberal government which delayed it for five years because it could not reach an understanding with the company involved.

But hon. members opposite wanted to make a political issue of it. A political issue is made of everything that is done by the Department of Public Works in every riding. This is not the way in which the people of Canada should be treated. I hope that some day the minister will visit my riding and be able to show that he is non-partisan. I have wished to say this for a long time, but this is the first opportunity I have had to do so.
I believe that very soon the officials of the department should begin to prepare themselves for the enormous urban development programs which will be required in the various large centres of this country. This department has a great responsibility. I hope in these days when there is a cutting back on expenditures and the people of Canada are being asked to go easy in their demands, that the minister now at least will begin to plan for a future which is not too far away; because in the future there will be a necessity to institute large and extensive projects in the urban areas of our country.
To this point I have made no request of the minister in respect of any projects in my riding, because I consider this to be something which should be brought up under the different items. I would remind the minister however, that the members of this party believe that the large expenditures on the part of the government must be stopped at this time, and priorities must be established. These priorities must be established in such a way that our citizens will not be deprived of the opportunity to earn income. I could cite a dozen cases where an expenditure of $200, $300 or $500 was refused when this expenditure would have made available facilities which would have enabled our fishermen to practise their trade and earn an income, so that they would not be obliged to go to the social services for help. This is one area in which I believe the Department of Public Works is falling down. It does not seem to be concerned about the small projects. At the present time it would appear that the department is mainly concerned with the large construction projects because small ones, such as the expenditure of $200 or $300 for dredging in order that three or four fishermen might be able to earn their living, are turned down. The type of spending the department is doing

Mr. Chairman, let me take the opportunity of making a few remarks tonight, during our consideration of these estimates, about a matter of considerable interest to the people of Vancouver. Before doing so let me congratulate the minister on the very fine job he has done this summer in making parliament hill a very gay and attractive place, with many flags and decorations during centennial year. I do not think Nelson at the battle of Trafalgar was more flag conscious than our Minister of Public Works when he decorated parliament hill this summer.
Over the past 20 years there has been a project being carried out by the Department of Public Works in the Vancouver area. This project, the Stanley park sea wall, that has cost very little but is of enormous attraction to the people of Vancouver, was discontinued during the course of this last year. I have received a great deal of correspondence, with respect to it, as have other hon. members who represent that city, from citizens of that area.
Stanley park is a body of land surrounded on three sides by water. It is actually an old piece of naval reserve property which was given to the city on a 99 year lease as a public park about the beginning of the century. Its name is virtually synonymous with the name of the city. Montreal has its Mount Royal; Ottawa has its parliament hill. I am not sure what Toronto has, but Vancouver has Stanley park. About 20 years ago the Department of Public Works began to build a sea wall and a footpath around the park along its shores. This was carried out each year on the suggestion that erosion was gradually chewing away at the cliffs of the parkland. Apparently it was decided that a

sea wall would arrest this erosion and justify the project.
Year by year the Department of Public Works in a modest way gradually extended one of the finest walks or footpaths in the world. This footpath extends through some of the most magnificent forest land in Canada, runs along the shore of English bay and around a corner in sight of Siwash rock. Many people who find little or no recreation other than walking have the opportunity of following this footpath and derive from it tremendous enjoyment. This area of Vancouver has in it a great number of older people in residence. The west end of Vancouver in which Stanley park lies is a haven for these elderly people, many of whom find their only activity and recreation in that park. It came as a shock to them this year to find that this project has been discontinued, on the ground, according to the department, that erosion was minimal. Let me suggest that no one in the city of Vancouver ever really felt that this path was being built because erosion was either maximal or minimal.
During this 20 year period Vancouverites have come to believe that the Department of Public Works was building one of the finest scenic footpaths in the world and that it would be continued. This path is something like two miles in length and, if completed, would join with footpaths along the inner harbour. I believe it is commendable to save money, but the Department of Public Works, apparently on those grounds alone, has decided to chisel on this project to the extent of the $35,000 which was to be spent this year. The department has used the excuse that erosion is minimal. I know of no other place where the work of the Department of Public Works or any other federal government works at such a low cost has brought more real pleasure to more people.
To complete this project would only involve the construction of a few hundred yards of sea wall and path. I should not like to think that the government, having almost completed this project, would really discontinue it and place a sign at the end, for the people to see to the effect that anyone who passes that point does so at his own risk. Having started this project 20 years ago I should like to think the department is prepared to complete it, because it is very attractive and has been constructed at very little cost, bringing tremendous pleasure to a great number of people.

Those are the remarks I wanted to make tonight. First of all I wanted to congratulate the minister for what I thought was a very fine display on parliament hill this year. Second, I urge him to complete the few hundred yards of this sea wall so as not to leave us with the idea in Vancouver that the federal government has let us down.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to answer some of the questions that have been asked. The hon. member for Gaspe spoke about protection walls, mainly on the St. Lawrence. I wanted to indicate that it is quite true that this type of wall has been constructed over very many years. There is in the St. Lawrence a situation whereby some erosion is caused by shipping. In those cases the federal government has felt it has reponsibility and has tried to continue the policy of erecting the necessary protection walls. There may be other reasons, due to the construction of a dock or wharf, where erosion may be caused and a similar rule would be applied. But where the erosion is from natural causes the federal government has taken the position that it is not a federal responsibility.
This is where the difficulty arises, because wherever there is erosion it seems that there is a tendency, and I can understand it very well, for those persons affected to feel that the federal government should immediately put in a protection wall, although the federal government does not have jurisdiction over the resource being eroded. In that case it falls with n the provincial or local field of responsibility. This is the reason for the difficulty on the subject of protective works.
The hon. member for Gaspe spoke about my not having been able to make the trip to his area. I regret that very, very much. I share his view about the desirability of making the trip, but so far it has not been possible. No one regrets that more than I do. As for the hon. member's remarks about the project at Chandler, that all-important project, I thought when he began his remarks, and indeed throughout more than half of them, that he was applying a delicious sense of humour and was making a humourous reference. But I fear that some of the interjections indicate that perhaps some members of the federal parliament have those sensitivities that some of us wish they did not have, and the hon. member was seeking to make sure that the people of Gaspe knew who had all the virtues and who had all the
Supply-Public Works vices. I myself would not want to indicate who has all the virtues and who has all the vices because my experience in life has led me to believe that it does not work out that one person gets them all. In any event, I have tried to examine the projects as they have come in from the Gaspe, and I would remind the hon. member, in all modesty, that he should not have made the claim that he did make about the Chandler project. It is true that this project was talked about for many years. It was a Liberal government that took the tough decision to go ahead with it. Whether it is a virtue or a vice, they did it, and it is not a useful exercise to claim here that a government that has been out of office for several years undertook the project, because the record simply does not support that thesis. I will leave it at that.
The hon. gentleman made a point that I think it is well to bear in mind at this time. He said that large government expenditures must be stopped and that priorities must be established. This is the situation in which we are working at the present time. No one knows better than I what is involved in curtailing expenditures. The matter of priorities comes into that consideration. We have had to set our minds very firmly on the path of curtailing expenditures, and we are doing this. It will raise questions of priorities. These have to be detailed very carefully so that those projects which will produce the most benefit to the area or the country are proceeded with, and the others, while important but of a less direct benefit to the community or the population as a whole, are deferred.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. gentleman indicate which projects in the present estimates are being deferred?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. Perhaps I can do it best by taking just one illustration which will make the point. I will give the committee a good example of it, namely, the parking garage on parliament hill. It was due for tender call for next month, November of this year. That is the best example I can give. I could detail others, but a good many were started and they cannot be stopped.
Why does the hon. gentleman pick the worst example?

The hon. member for Carleton can imagine that this hon. gentleman had some feelings on the subject and adopted the course with very great reluctance. He can be
