Mr. Chairman, I will be quite brief because I know there are hon. members here who want to raise certain points of interest to their constituents. In view of the limited time we have for the discussion of estimates I would like to make a suggestion to the minister. Instead of taking 15 or 20 minutes to answer the representations made by two hon. members-which I think is quite normal under usual circumstances-I suggest he listen to hon. members' representations and then write each one a letter later on, when he has more time.
Or better still, change the rules to allow more time for the discussion of estimates.

I rise to speak briefly
because I have been in close association with this department and I have known the officers in charge of public works in Kootenay for over 60 years. On numerous occasions I have inspected for them wharves which were built on contract, or breakwaters or piles which were driven in, and things of that sort. So this is familiar ground to me. I am more of a builder than an intellectual. What I will say is by way of representations made by an old backwoodsman after meeting his constituents in the summer holidays.
First of all I wish to say that I appreciate the minister's response to any matters I brought to his attention. The same is true of the senior officials in Ottawa, the district officials in Vancouver and the local officials in the district, until they retired a short time ago. I must say that I found the Department of Public Works very fair indeed. I cannot complain of partisanship.
Are they good for a new wharf?

Whether it was the Liberal or the Conservative government that was in office, I have always been treated very fairly. I go around and meet the various organizations and groups and find out what is required. I have never asked for things I do
October 30, 1967

not think are necessary. Then I go to Vancouver and talk it over with the district officers there. Finally I come to Ottawa and make a brief plea here. We treat public works on a non-partisan basis in my district.
I do want to mention to the minister that the development of the Columbia river has created an entirely new set of circumstances, so it is only possible to plan for two or three years ahead until the whole matter has settled down and the necessary improvements have been decided upon.
I do urge that in the rebuilding of these facilities a local employee be employed to look after the immediate maintenance of certain wharves and things of that sort. Recently a man who was in charge in the district retired, and someone from the Okanagan is now in charge of the Kootenay area. It meant that in some cases wharves became quite unsafe, a plank would go out on a wharf or a piling would go down, and there was no one to repair it immediately. I understand this matter is being given consideration, so that some local person who has experience will look after these immediate needs in the repair of wharves, the clearing of driftwood from wharves in high water, and things of that sort.
I am informed that a number of wharves have been flooded out on the Arrow lakes and the Columbia river and it is the responsibility of the British Columbia power authority to pay for the replacement of the wharves in the new communities that will be established. I suggest that the department work in co-operation with the British Columbia hydro and that it make certain before coming to any final decision that a wharf is required, because of the number of people left in the community. I have heard that in some cases there was no intention to build a wharf because only a couple of dozen people were left in that community.
I suggest that the departmental officials pay very close attention to the development going on at the present time, and before coming to any final decision make sure that any docks built are built where they are required, even though the population may be quite small under the present circumstances.
I suggest also that in the meantime the dredge on the Arrow lakes be maintained. It is not expected to dredge, in view of the rising of the water, when the High Arrow dam is completed, but I do suggest the department maintain the dredge in the meantime because when the High Arrow dam is completed there may be certain work
Supply-Public Works for the dredge to do in maintaining channels into the new wharves, or possibly dredging certain channels from one area to another. This dredge will also be very useful for rental at a per diem rate to organizations or communities which want to use it in the building of their own projects, such as launching facilities for clubs. It has been usual for the department throughout the years to rent this dredge for around $50 a day to non-profit community organizations developing community projects. I suggest the dredge be maintained at the present time which, under present circumstances, simply means keeping a watch on it, because it may be used when the projects are completed for the dredging of approaches to the wharves which will be rebuilt later under the department's jurisdiction and instruction, and for certain other breakwaters that may be required.
I want to bring to the minister's attention the fact that the development going on in our district will provide a great opportunity for recreational development, and the consequent development of the tourist industry because of the large amount of lake frontage available. I am told that in the Kootenays we have the largest area on the North American continent of front shore property on a lake or a river close to transportation. I can also quote the former leader of the official opposition, who spent several days in the Kootenays during the summer recess. When he left the district the hon. member for Prince Albert said he could not understand why the finest district in Canada was not advertised more than it is at the present time. This is my prelude to further suggestions.
As I said before, I go around and meet the village councils, boards of trade, women's institutes and other organizations. I must tell you that I like meeting women because I have always found them very constructive, especially if they are of the type that understand the things we are talking about. I met the Ainsworth boat club at Ainsworth Hot Springs. They have already commenced building a marina for the tying up of the boats coming in for tourist purposes. The tourist industry there is very large and I think they have already spent something in the neighbourhood of $10,000 or so. I understand that departmental officials have looked at this project and will give them some assistance. This is not a large expenditure. It is a small marina which will be of great advantage in developing the recreational

I do not propose to take up too much time of the committee, but I feel I just cannot allow this opportunity to pass without urging upon the minister the importance of trying to impress upon the Minister of Finance that he should not make the Northumberland strait crossing a casualty of operation broadaxe. We know of course that every time the Minister of Public Works speaks on this subject he assures the people of Prince Edward Island that the crossing will not be abandoned. However, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that that is not good enough. The people of Prince Edward Island want to know now when the project is going to be started and when it is going to be completed.
When this project was announced in 1965, the government committed itself to the spending of $30 million a year over a five year period until the project was completed. 
Now, Mr. Chairman, neither $30 million nor anything like it has been spent as yet and the people of our province are looking to the government to honour the commitment made to them in 1965. I agree with the hon. member for Gaspe and with the Minister of Finance that, under present circumstances, large public expenditures have to be cut back. I suggest, however, that some system of priorities must be established.
We have to argue the merits of this causeway, and one of the bases of this argument would be that our province requires it economically. I do not believe this would be difficult to establish. If one takes a look at the statistics he finds that Prince Edward Island has the lowest per capita earnings of any province in Canada. Something must be done to close the economic gap between our province and the other provinces of Canada. Everybody who has made a study of the economy of the Atlantic area over the past number of years has recognized that there is a large economic gap. They have looked for the key to close this gap. I suggest the key to close the gap is the construction of the causeway. There can be no real improvement in the per capita income of the people of Prince Edward Island, and that is what we need, unless we have easy and continuous access to the markets of the other provinces.
Prince Edward Island has fought long and hard for this causeway. Prince Edward Island stayed out of confederation from 1867 to 1873 mainly because her transportation problems had not been resolved satisfactorily. In 1873 we did enter confederation on the understanding-and this was written into the terms of union which I will quote-that we would be guaranteed efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers, to be established and maintained between the island and the mainland, winter and summer, thus placing the island in continuous communication with the Intercolonial Railway and the railway system of the dominion.
Up until the present time, these terms of confederation have not been fulfilled because the ferry service is not adequate to give us continuous communication with the mainland. At one time Prince Edward Island was so dissatisfied she felt she had an action against the federal government for a breach of the terms of union. The province actually sued the federal government for something like $17 million and was able to obtain a judgment for about a million dollars. This judgment is recorded and can be seen by

anyone who wants to take the trouble to look it up.
We consider that the terms of union have not been fulfilled. I suggest that this causeway has been a political football for too long, and for too long have we suffered by reason of the fact the causeway has been made a political football. Feasibility studies were commenced in 1956. When those studies were completed in 1962, the then prime minister of Canada, Mr. Diefenbaker, announced that the causeway would be built. I am confident that had the Conservative government remained in power the causeway would be almost completed today. However, this did not happen. In 1962 we had a minority government, and unfortunately in 1963 the Conservative government was defeated and the Liberal government took power.
Good government.

Good government? Let us see what happened to the causeway. On July 8,	1965, the present Prime Minister
announced that tenders would be called. He called a press conference and I should like to quote from the press report:
Prime Minister Pearson announced today that tenders will be called later this year tor a combined tunnel, bridge and causeway between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
Construction is expected to start next April.
I do not know to which April he was referring, but apparently that April has not come as yet.
Construction is expected to start next April and Mr. Pearson said at a press conference he hopes it will be completed in late 1970.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I want the Minister of Public Works to assure this house and the people of Prince Edward Island that the expectation expressed by the Prime Minister in July, 1965, will be fulfilled, and that this causeway will be completed in 1970. The press report goes on to say that when the Prime Minister made the announcement he was flanked by new mines minister J. Watson MacNaught, Prince Edward Island cabinet representative, and works minister George Mcllraith, the same man occupies the position of Minister of Public Works today.
Then, they picked the mines minister, Mr. MacNaught, up from the bowels of the earth, brushed the coal dust off his feet and sent him over to Prince Edward Island to announce to the people that the Liberal government was going to build the causeway. Mr. MacNaught flew to Prince Edward Island in a Department 27053-232
Supply-Public Works of Transport Viscount to make the announcement to the people of Prince Edward Island, and when making the announcement he was flanked by huge diagrams of the proposed project.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
We have seen these diagrams ever since 1956. I ask the Minister of Public Works to tell his men to put their crayons back in the boxes and give us something to walk on instead of pictures. We are sick to death of looking at pictures of the proposed causeway. Mr. MacNaught, flanked by these pictures, said at the time this was a proud moment for him to be in his native province and to indicate that finally the dreams of the people were about to be realized. He said a project of this magnitude was above politics and there was absolutely no connection between the announcement and any plans the government may have for an election in the near future. This was in August, 1965, and it just so happened there was an election in November of the same year.
Then, not satisfied with that, and perhaps believing the people of our province were not convinced, the government sent down the master of them all, the then minister of transport. He is a man who in opposition always championed the cause of the people of Prince Edward Island, but who when he joined the government was not listened to so attentively. However, the then minister of transport ran up and down the island like a dog looking for a telephone pole. Everywhere he stopped he assured the people that the causeway would be built. Then in October 1965, exactly one month before the election, he said in Kensington that there would be no further hold-ups. Mark that, Mr. Chairman-no further hold-ups.
He ran out of poles.

He said that the work was being pushed ahead. According to him, this was not to be a gift to Prince Edward Island. This was not an election bribe, but a sound economic investment for Canada. We want to know now where this sound economic investment for Canada is.
It is growing very rapidly.

If it was a sound economic investment one month before the November 1965 election, I suggest it is a sound economic investment now and must not become a victim of operation broadaxe.

Then the minister of external affairs-yes, Mr. Chairman, they loaded their big guns and sent them down-came to the island on October 26, two weeks before the election, and he told the people of the island that this causeway would do more to stimulate economic growth in Prince Edward Island than anything since confederation. And did that ever go over good, Mr. Chairman.
Then the minister of mines was sent down to the island with his bulldozer, a couple of days before the election, and he started the road; but that is practically all we have heard of this causeway since then.
The hon. member should get his facts straight.

Nothing concrete has been done since. We want some action. Let me say to hon. gentlemen across the way: Come alive, get on to yourselves. They have no seats in Prince Edward Island, and they will get none the next time if they do not do something to build this causeway. We want the causeway before the next election; we want something to be done right away.
I agree there are people who argue against the causeway on the basis that it is too expensive. I am half inclined to believe that the government itself is coming to the conclusion that it will cost too much money. All I can say, Mr. Chairman, is that that is not a valid argument. Some people would like to divide the number of people on the island into the cost of the causeway, and to point out that it will cost so much per capita; but I contend that this approach is ridiculous.
This is a causeway that will benefit not only the people of Prince Edward Island but all people in Canada. Even if it did benefit only the people of Prince Edward Island, they are still entitled to it. We are a province of Canada and want to be joined to Canada. There are provinces today asking to be separated from Canada; all we want is to be given the chance to be joined to Canada and to become part of this great country.
When people say the causeway will cost too much, did anybody complain about the $350 million to build the St. Lawrence seaway? For example, who today complains about the Columbia river development in British Columbia? Who complains about the Mactaquac in New Brunswick? Who complains about the atomic power establishments in Ontario and Manitoba. No one. These projects are all part of our national investment. Therefore, no one should complain about the cost of the causeway to Prince

Edward Island. We need it, it is necessary for our economic development.
Mr. Churchill, who apparently is now an agent of the Department of Public Works, set the thing out very clearly, I think, when he spoke in Charlottetown a few days ago, and I should like to place on record what he said at that time:
The cost of building and operating the nine mile Northumberland strait crossing could be recovered within 50 years.
That is true, Mr. Chairman. The ferry is today operating at an annual deficit of $5 million. At a loss of $5 million a year, within 50 years the causeway would be paid for. Mr. Churchill continued:
But even without such savings, the benefit to the isolated economy of Prince Edward Island, now joined to the mainland by ferry service, could be enormous.
"I am tempted to believe that there can be no real improvement in income and standards of living on the island unless easy and continuous access to markets is arranged"-
I say amen to that.
"As a Canadian project, the crossing will rank with construction of the St. Lawrence Seaway,"-
Although it would cost less to construct than the $550 million Churchill falls power project in Labrador, "the technical problems appear more difficult."
Despite the difficulties of building in the ocean and despite heavy costs to the federal government, "less tangible benefits might be found in the effect on the general business climate in eastern Canada and the renewed interest that might be shown in locating in the Atlantic region."
"I think these points are perhaps not given the weight they should have when people consider the economics of providing the crossing"-
"If the economy of this island is improved to the point where reduction of federal subsidies to the provincial government in the amount of only $5 million a year can be achieved, capital and capitalized operation of the crossing might well be recovered within 50 years-
Any difference that now exists between the wage earnings in Prince Edward Island and the rest of the region or of Canada will tend to be equalized during the period of heavy labour demand occasioned by the construction itself"-
That is what Mr. Churchill had to say, Mr. Chairman. As far as we can find out, Mr. Churchill is an accredited representative of the Department of Public Works, and he says that the causeway will be of terrific economic advantage to our province.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I should like to urge upon the government as strongly as I can to delay this project no more, because if they do they will be in trouble with the people of Prince Edward Island.
Ociober 30, 1967
It has not been delayed at all.

It has. The minister continues to say that the project has not been delayed, yet when the project was announced in 1965 the government of the day promised to spend $30 million per year over a five year period.
It did not. See the text of the press release.

The government promised that $30 million a year would be spent. As a matter of fact, I have the press release here if I can take the time to look it up. The minister now says that the project is not being delayed. We cannot see any real, sincere effort being made to construct the causeway at the present time. Two years have passed since 1965, and although the minister promises that the causeway will be built we want him to announce now when construction is going to start in earnest. Then and only then will the people of Prince Edward Island be satisfied that this government has lived up to the promise it made early in 1965.

Mr. Chairman, I have two or three items on the public works estimates that I should like to mention; they are mostly constituency problems.
I am one of the members of this house who has respect for the Minister of Public Works, mostly because of the co-operation I have received from him in the many requests I have made in the house during the short time I have been here. I took the opportunity to say as much when I was given the job of introducing the minister at an official function at the opening of our new arena, a centennial project in Clinton this past year.
Might I say that the people of Bayfield are sincerely grateful for the reconstruction of the north pier, part of the cost of which appears in the estimates last year, the remainder being in these estimates. The job is either completed or close to completion.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The success of the project was marred by an accident in which two local boys lost their lives. We were all saddened. I am sure that the accident was not caused through any negligence on the part of the department.
Another item I wish to speak about is the reconstruction at Snug Harbour, in Goderich. This reconstruction was promised as an election promise in the election previous to that of 1965. Because of the publicity this 27053-2325
Supply-Public Works announcement received at that time I followed it through. I am happy to say that the contract, which was also on the estimates of last year, was finally let on May 17 of this year. It is to reconstruct the Snug Harbour pier, and the estimated cost was $130,000. The actual cost will be over $186,000. Work is under way and should be completed shortly, and for that I thank the minister. I also wish to thank him for another $270,000, to be set beside the original $130,000, which will make up the $400,000 to be spent this year on Goderich harbour.
Goderich is about 20 miles from where I live, is one of the largest towns in the riding, and has a fair volume of vessel traffic. The $270,000 is required for reconstruction of the outer end of the north pier. Steel sheet piling and reinforced concrete are to be used, as this section now is in a state of deterioration, and concrete sections along the south face occasionally are falling into channels. During the spring run-off the Maitland river flows partly underneath the existing structure. The proposed work will consist of reconstructing a 640 foot long section of the north pier in steel sheet piling and reinforced concrete.
I received a press release earlier with regard to the reconstruction at Snug Harbour. It advised us that the contract had been let, at an estimated cost of $270,000. I wish to know when the work is to be completed, or if it has been completed. I have faith enough in the minister to know that if he has not that information, he will advise me as soon as possible when he has it.
I wanted to bring this matter to the minister's attention. I realize that this item is in the estimates, but I am anxious to see this work carried out. I also wanted to take the opportunity of thanking the minister for the co-operation he has extended to me during the short time I have been a member of this house.

I wish to address a few remarks to the Minister of Public Works, and to clarify something that has arisen recently. First of all, I may say to the hon. member for Kings that, in speaking on this matter for Renfrew county tonight, Renfrew county is larger than Prince Edward Island. If we had four members of parliament and four senators representing Renfrew county, we would have had a majority government from the beginning of this parliament.

Hear, hear.

Don't be too sure of that.
They might not have got in.

During the past several
months several meetings have taken place between officials of the town of Pembroke, officials of the Department of Public Works and the minister. The intention has been to demolish the dock that was built shortly after the first world war, the estimated cost of the demolition being between $90,000 and $100,000. This demolition has been badly needed for the past few years, as the dock has presented a great hazard to the area.
Recent estimates show an amount of $50,000 set aside for the demolition of this wharf. So that the officials of Pembroke will be fully aware of the department's plan with regard to this wharf, I wish to ask the minister whether it is the intention to have an additional amount of money included in the estimates for the year 1968-69 to complete this job satisfactorily to both parties concerned.
The simple answer is yes, Mr. Chairman.

If in the remarks I intend to make I sound repetitive, I make no apologies whatever. On the contrary, I can assure hon. members opposite that I shall continue to hammer away at these subjects until the constituents I represent get some satisfaction and consideration in connection with the problems they are facing.
Speaking on the estimates of the Department of Industry I made an appeal to the Minister of Industry assuming he was as interested in keeping industries from going to the wall, or disappearing for lack of certain facilities, as he was in encouraging new industries. I got no reply. Then, sotto voce, I heard him mention my constituency when he said he intended to reply only to those members who were sufficiently interested to remain in their seats. I can assure the minister that I was in my place when he began his remarks, I was there while he was making them and I was still there when he concluded. I have not heard from him.
Accordingly I intend to start with another minister because it is my purpose to try, somehow or other, to get some co-ordination into the conglomerate government we have opposite-ministers who apparently do not speak to each other or who never bother to relate economic factors in the slightest degree.
Long before the Minister of Finance announced that expenditures should be curtailed, and before it became apparent to him

that deficit financing would inevitably contribute to the inflation we are now facing, I was among the first to recognize the realities of the situation. However, when curtailing expenditure I maintain that cuts should not be made where the economy is feeblest. These are the areas which must be sustained, while cuts are made in the more exotic and less fruitful expenditures that I observe going on in the country.
The hon. member for Gaspd said he had hoped to see the Minister of Public Works in his constituency this summer but was disappointed because that hon. gentleman failed to arrive there. Well, I am informed that the minister did visit my constituency. I never saw him, though. When I learned he was there, and went to Yarmouth, he had disappeared although he had in tow a group of political lame ducks and other characters who were liable to become lame ducks because their constituencies would disappear as a result of redistribution. I hope this will ease the soul of my hon. friend from Gaspe in some sort of way: it probably would not have made a bit of difference, to have had a ministerial visit.
My constituency depends principally on the fisheries, on tourism and on the secondary industry which is slowly developing there. I want to place the emphasis now on fisheries. I should like to draw attention to some of the more glaring difficulties which we are at present disenjoying-there are many others, but time will not permit me to go into them-by putting forward a brief catalogue of these highlights in geographical succession. On Christmas day last year the new wharf at Saulnierville was washed out by a very bad storm. As far as I know, nothing has been done to repair it. We are now approaching another winter of storms. Having had some background in engineering and some experience in construction also, I would say this is a bad situation because the storm which wrecked the wharf in the first place may well be succeeded by an even more severe one this year and I hardly think that a damaged wharf will stand up to another severe attack.
I ask the minister what he is planning to do. I look at the estimates, realizing of course that the estimates for the year did not anticipate this brand new wharf going to pieces. I look at the supplementary estimates and I see not a cent for the repair of this wharf. Apparently the minister's motto is that of Wilhelm II of Germany-"Gott mit uns."
Supply-Public Works Mr. Chairman, this wharf is the basis upon which the fishing industry in the northern part of Clare operates. With its disappearance hundreds and hundreds of men will be deprived of an opportunity to earn their livelihood in the one business they know.

I drop down the coast now to the Mete-ghan river, one of the few semi-natural harbours on the exposed coast of St. Mary's bay. This is the site of a large shipbuilding industry. This port has been neglected. With a relatively modest investment it could be revived and placed in such a condition that the shipyard company would be able to rig their vessels after they are launched and conduct repair jobs. The company to which I am referring has had on the stocks at one time eight big ships, and employs about 180 men. I see nothing in the estimates, supplementary or otherwise, which indicates that any effort is being made to revive what once was a very fine little harbour. This harbour could play a very vital role in the economy of Clare.
There is another matter which I have mentioned previously to the minister, and in the house, and that is the situation in Yarmouth. Some two or three years ago a very fine public wharf was built at Yarmouth. Today it is dangerously overcrowded. Large purse seiners have been built in the last year or two and they are crowded in at the wharf seven or eight deep. If one of these should explode in the middle of one of these clusters, the whole fleet might go up in flames and there could be a real catastrophe. Certainly they are crowded to the point where effective operations cannot be carried out.
Here again we have an example of an industry in this constituency which, although on the point of being developed, is being restricted because of inadequate infrastructure. I have proposed to the minister and also to the house the idea of acquiring the old Evangeline wharf property which has been abandoned for a number of years. The wharf no longer is suitable but the site is one which could be used appropriately for another wharf. I do not see any evidence of any move being taken in this direction. The first thing to do would be to acquire the property. Then a wharf could be built which would enable the people in the area to take part in the fisheries which are being developed in the area. I am always told such things as: Oh, well, we are digging a basin out there. I

Supply-Public Works should like to read about this marvellous basin. This is an article in The Light Herald of Yarmouth dated September 28, 1967:
The dredging of the inner basin at the public wharf which began this spring, was expected to provide some relief for small seiners by deepening the basin to 12 feet. The government has informed me that the policy now is not to have a "wharf for every fisherman" but rather to have a number of large strategically located fishing ports. Certainly Yarmouth is qualified to benefit from such a policy, but nothing is being done.
I should like to move on now to Cape Sable island which traditionally for many years has been one of the great fishing areas on our coast. Here there is a real need for a deep water wharf so that the plants on Cape Sable island may be supplied with fish by the big off-shore ships. Cape Sable island has 3,500 to 4,000 people who obtain their living from the sea. About 4,000 more people on the mainland derive their living from the Cape Sable islanders activities. This wharf has been the subject of a great deal of argument, but no appropriations have been made and no building projects have been undertaken. The whole matter has developed into the chicken and egg sort of argument, in which it is said that if the companies put in the plants the wharf will be built, and the companies say they will not build the plants until they see the wharf. In the meantime my understanding is that there is already a surplus fish processing capacity on the island and that this would warrant a start being made on the wharf. If this is done, then we will see the processors move in with additional plant.
In so far as Shelburne is concerned, it has one of the most magnificent harbours on the

Atlantic coast. At one time it was a great centre for yachting. Hundreds of yachts from the United States used to put in at this port. Supplies were purchased and this provided considerable business for the merchants in the town. At the present time there is a good public wharf there, but it is util, zed entirely by the fishing industry. There is not a wharf at which a yacht could tie up. A breakwater-wharf should be built on the west side of Shelburne harbour. The town has already acquired a shore property and this they would be disposed to turn over to the government if the government would put in the facility I have mentioned.
I should like to point out to hon. members that the constituency of Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare is the largest fishing constituency in the whole of Canada. The landed value of the fish is the greatest. We are speaking of a major industry which is being throttled because of the lack of repairs in some cases, the enlargement of existing facilities in other cases and the construction of needed new elements in the infrastructure. I should like to quote again from The Light Herald of September 28. While the statement which I should like to quote refers in particular to Yarmouth, it applies to all the areas I have mentioned:
The hopes of the town lie with the board of trade, and if their action is not successful in getting action from the Departments of Transport and Public Works for additional facilities along the waterfront, the government can look forward to having the fishing industry of Western Nova Scotia turn into another Cape Breton coal industry where the costs to rescue the area from economic ruin will far exceed that of aiding our fishing industry now.

Mr. Chairman, there has been much conversation here about cutting expenditures and slashing the estimates. Apropos of this fact I think I should point out that part of the reason for these large government expenditures can be associated with certain cabinet ministers lauding as something virtuous, the large amounts of money under their authority and expended by this departments. I have read press statements in which cabinet ministers have from time to time extolled the tremendous contributions they are making to Canada because of the large sums of money they control. Let me hasten to add that I have not read any such press statements issued by the Minister of Public Works. Some of his colleagues have very hefty propaganda machines in their offices for this purpose.
October 30, 1967

The government is at fault here for not expressing concern about the value received from the money expended or from what has been accomplished. The members of the cabinet simply refer to the large amounts under their control. References are made to previous years to show the millions of dollars more to be spent by their departments in the current year. They do so in an attempt to develop some sort of political support for the degree to which they spend the public money.
We should expect a different set of responsibilities than those expressed so far, in that the government should cut back on the spending of some of these spendthrifts who are not so much concerned with the welfare of the public as they are in how much money they can spend, in the manner of the often referred to drunken sailor. These huge expenditures seem also to be associated with a claim for pol.tical support. The Department of Public Works falls heir to this sort of exploitation. Members of constituencies who happen to be representative of the party in government also laud the virtue of high government expenditure on public works within their own constituencies, and demand such expenditures on the basis of gaining additional political support.
All of this misuse of public funds leads to the situation we face today, in which the Minister of Finance is sharpening his axe to the proper hone in order to slash, slice and slit the estimates of every department; and one he is aiming at is the Department of Public Works. I am sure the minister knows this very well. His department may have relatively little impact upon some urban constituencies. Earlier I asked some of my colleagues in the house from urban ridings what effect public works spending meant to them. They had to grope and think, but eventually arrived at the answer that post offices and federal buildings represent the extent of public works spending.
The expenditures of this department have a tremendous impact on constituencies which I represent and the constituency represented by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare, as well as those of other coastal or maritime areas where the men work in the fishing or shipping trades. In these areas breakwaters, wharves, docks and floats are all of tremendous assistance, both to the economy of the area and the safety of the workers.
Let me give you an example of the value of public works projects to these areas, both
Supply-Public Works from the point of view of the number of projects and the value to politicians in the area. I am sure this is true in certain communities in Skeena and other parts of my constituency. Let me show one example of what I have in mind.
Prior to the 1962 election the public works estimates contained an appropriation for a breakwater at the Indian community of Kiti-mat. This project was approved in 1962, according to the officials within the department. You will remember that during that year the then prime minister returned following the election and said that things were in a terrible state, and that the government had to curtail public works expenditure. Apparently this had something to do with the extremely dangerous balance of payments situation. Various projects provided for in the estimates of the Department of Public Works and other departments were cut.
The Indian community to which I have referred depends to a great extent on fishing, and depends for safety upon adequate breakwaters. They had a breakwater almost within their grasp in 1962, but lost it because of some financial difficulties the federal government faced. The appropriation for that project did not find its way back into the estimates until this year, five years later. What sort of system of revision and priorities must exist within a department such as this? What sort of planning must take place? How can any community have admiration or respect for a department or government when they realize that a worth-while project such as this, having once been approved, is cut out because of financial problems of the government of the day? Perhaps they accept this as being one of those things which occur, but having to wait for five years before the project comes back within reach is something that should not happen.
Let me say that this project is being proceeded with at the moment, for completion sometime next spring. There do not appear to be any impediments in the way of its completion. Surely there should be greater understanding of the responsibility of government to communities such as the one to which I have referred. I am sure that the situation in respect of this project has been duplicated in many other areas. Many projects have probably reached a certain stage of priority only to be cut back for some financial reason, and presumably lost in the shuffle which goes on within the department.

Mr. Speaker, my question on the adjournment proceedings arises out of a statement of the first list of geographical co-ordinates establishing the straight base lines for purposes of demarking our territorial seas and fishing zones. In this matter Canada has acted, in my view, in accordance with the practices and the conventions of international law, and throughout we have negotiated and consulted with the nations that historically have fished within the waters which we will be endeavouring to enclose within our territorial and fishing zones. In particular we have negotiated throughout with the United States and have assured them of their historic and treaty rights. But the United States has protested the Canadian position, and the United States protest and rejection of our position is in my view unacceptable. It is on this matter that my question arose. I hope it is equally unacceptable to the fishermen and the congressmen from the states of Alaska, Washington and Oregon who have as much at stake in the establishment of the concept of straight base lines and territorial and fishing zones as we in Canada have.
Canada has no alternative in this matter but to enforce the law as it has been passed by this sovereign parliament and enacted by regulation of the cabinet of Canada. However, coming from the west coast as I do I am particularly concerned about and interested in Canada's jurisdiction over the Dixon entrance, the Hecate strait and Queen Charlotte sound. First we are entitled to a full
DEBATES	3667
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion and frank statement from the government outlining the future of these waters, and second, before such a statement is made- and this is why I rose the other day-I want once again to impress upon the government that we on the west coast want the fisheries jurisdiction over these waters, and I am quite sure will be satisfied with nothing else. We are primarily but not exclusively concerned with our salmon stocks which spawn in our rivers and range far out to sea. It is essential in the long term that we have a treaty binding all the nations fishing in the Pacific, providing for the protection and conservation of those fisheries stocks. But I am not an optimist and I do not see such a treaty being agreed upon in the very near future. In the meantime we require as an absolute essential fisheries jurisdiction over the waters I have mentioned.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Some internationalists tell me that we will never be able to establish as a principle of international law that these waters can be the territorial waters of Canada. May I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we are interested, and I speak for myself, really only in the fisheries protection aspect of these waters, and not the other aspects of sovereignty over these waters, such as the right to defence. We are solely concerned with our fisheries jurisdiction over these waters. If we cannot gain acceptance by international law of these other territorial jurisdictions over waters, may I suggest to the government that they attempt to work out a deal with the other nation involved under which we could draw base lines, including those waters for fisheries jurisdiction only. I believe this would be acceptable to me and to the fishermen at home whose livelihood is related to this question. I believe the Russians and the Japanese will be encroaching upon these waters. We are not so much concerned that they should be the territorial waters of Canada, but we are concerned that they be protected by Canada for fisheries purposes. If we cannot work out a deal one way, may I suggest we try to work out a deal by which these waters become protected for fisheries purposes only?

FRETGHT RATES-CREAM-REQUEST FOR RESCISSION OF RECENT INCREASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if you had been in the habit of travelling from your apartment building by bus, how would you like it if one morning you were told that instead of paying a 25 cent fare normally charged, the fare would be $2.50? If you were in the habit of travelling by car, how would you like to drive to the service station and instead of being charged 45 cents for a gallon of gasoline be requested to pay $4.50 in order that you may continue to use your car? My question this morning was directed to the Minister of Agriculture


(Mr. Greene), although it did relate to problems which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) must resolve. I wanted to know what the government was doing about rescinding an order issued by the transport commission which allows the railways to charge a 1,000 per cent higher rate for the shipment of cream. From a charge of 65 cents to deliver a can of cream to the creamery and back, the railways are now allowed to charge up to $6.35 and more. After several trips to and from the creamery you might as well throw away that can. It costs about $11 or $12 for the can, and after four trips, as I say, you might as well throw it away.
They say that power corrupts, and the more absolute the power the more absolute the corruption. That may not be entirely true of the commission, but when parliament authorized the board of transport commissioners to permit a reorganization of the railways and dealt with the transportation bill, I stated at the time that it was not a transportation bill but a railway bill. The bill was not going to solve our transportation problems; it was going to try to solve the problems of the railways.
Perhaps the railways are going to be happy with this new rate, but I suggest that the commission has gone hog-wild in allowing the railways to charge such a ridiculous rate as this. If this rate proves exorbitant to the users of the railway, then what revenue can the railways possibly derive from it?
In Saskatchewan it is estimated there are between 1,500 and 2,000 cream shippers who will go out of business. They will not be able to ship their cream by truck; they normally depend on the railways. They depend on a few trucks to ship their cream and maintain their farm operation.
Many of them pay the fuel bills for their tractors and cars with money earned the hard way. They get up early at dawn to milk the cows, and send off their cream before the kids go to school on the bus. Then after the kids come back from school they milk the cows, well on into the night. These are the people who will have to pay $6.35 on their cream.
The members of the commission who have made this order arrive at their offices at eight or nine in the morning, even ten o'clock, and at four or five o'clock their day is finished. The man who allowed himself to be appointed commissioner receives $40,000 a year. I asked the former minister of transport last
October 30, 1987

July when he was going to appoint a commission which would put some teeth into a provision to retain some rail lines, and more particularly to replace the bridge which had been destroyed west of Chelan. The minister said at the time that he hoped this would be done some time in September. I am sure he was aware then that he was going to be appointed to his new post, and when I asked this question I did not realize that we were going to end up with a commission which had the fangs of a werewolf. I did not realize it would consist of people who were willing to sacrifice hundreds of farmers who were trying to make a living the hard way.
This afternoon we spent a lot of time discussing the estimates of the Department of Industry, a department that does not seem to be aware of Parkinson's law. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Mackenzie has brought a serious matter before the house. It is too serious to be discussed in the language the hon. member has used this evening. To indulge in personalities, as the hon. member has, will not solve any problem.
I wish to tell him that I, too, know something about rising at four o'clock in the morning and milking cows. I have had a good deal of experience in these occupations and am in complete sympathy with the farmers. But this is no way to solve their problems.
I wish to tell the hon. member that the minister of agriculture of Saskatchewan brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture of Canada back on October 5. Of course the minister has also corresponded with the farmers, who are still getting up somewhat earlier than the hon. member for Mackenzie gets up.
The matter has been taken up with the Express Traffic Association of Canada by the director of traffic of the railway transport committee of the Canadian Transport Commission. The whole question of express rates on cream and returning empties was the subject of a review by senior express officials on October 24 and 25. The Minister of Transport hopes to be in a position to advise further within a week or ten days.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.25 p.m.

Tuesday. October 31. 1967
